members.author: yaowubarbara
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #2654: Both touch the exact same line in stdio.py — the write_stream (and read_stream) memory-object-stream buffer size, which defaults to 0 (unbuffered). clusters.pick_reason: #3243 replaces `anyio.Lock` with `anyio.Semaphore(1, max_value=1)` specifically because httpx can resume or close the auth-flow generator from a different task than the one that acquired the lock; `anyio.Lock` enforces same-task release and can raise at runtime in that scenario, while #2858 and #3252 keep `anyio.Lock` and remain exposed to it. #3243 and #2858 both add a second lock for single-flight refresh/auth-flow transitions (`flow_lock` vs. `refresh_lock`) separate from the per-request lock; #3252 instead keeps only the single original lock and restructures where in `async_auth_flow` it is acquired/released around the yield point, without adding single-flight semantics for concurrent refreshes.

clusters.pick_reason: Both PRs add a 'reject duplicate in-flight request id' check in _handle_post_request, but #3221 replaces the routing key itself (str(id) -> _request_stream_key()) rather than just gating on the old key. #3063's check keys off `str(request_id)` in `_request_streams`, which still collapses JSON-RPC id `1` (int) and `"1"` (string) into the same dict key — a numeric id in flight would falsely 409 a distinct string id, and a same-looking id of different type wouldn't be distinguished. It also leaves open a theoretical collision between `str(request_id)` and the reserved `GET_STREAM_KEY` sentinel used for the standalone GET stream. #3221's `_request_stream_key()` is type-preserving (`i:`/`s:` prefixes) and its docstring explicitly rules out both of those edge cases, so it's a strict superset fix applied to the same code path and error condition.
